title: Elodie and the Hymn
premise: Folklorist Oscar Amberdale arrives in the dying village of Hollowmere to record its last residents before a development company buys them out, but her sleep-activated recorder begins capturing a second voice — something that answers questions no one asked aloud. The voice belongs to what the village took in 1974: a girl named Elodie, drowned by her own family to seal a bargain that kept Hollowmere fed and hidden for fifty years. As Oscar's recordings unravel the pact, the villagers' memories begin bleeding into hers, and she realizes Elodie chose her because she carries the same name and the same hunger to be remembered. To end it, Oscar must return the hymnbook torn from Elodie's hands the night she died — buried under the chapel floor — before the final resident signs the sale papers and the village's memory is erased forever. In the flooded dark beneath the chapel, Oscar gives the book back and takes Elodie's place as the thing that remembers, while Hollowmere, finally unbound, is allowed to be forgotten.
about_author: Orsen Villalobos is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing oral histories from villages scheduled for demolition across northern England. He writes horror about the violence of being forgotten, and claims he has never once slept through a recording session since.

chapters.title: The Village That Refused an Encore
chapters.summary: Oscar Amberdale's POV. She arrives in Hollowmere with recording equipment and professional skepticism, interviewing elderly residents who sing each folk song exactly once and refuse repeats. The emotional beat is quiet unease: everyone is polite, cooperative, and visibly relieved when she leaves their kitchens.

chapters.title: Sleep Recordings
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. She leaves her recorder running overnight in her rented room at the Grey Lamb inn and wakes to find forty minutes of herself talking in her sleep — and a second voice, thin and young, answering questions she never asked. She tells herself it's radio interference. The beat: rationalization straining at the seams.

chapters.title: Mrs. Tallow's Version
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The oldest resident, Mrs. Tallow, hums four bars of a hymn then stops cold, hands shaking, and says 'we don't sing that twice' — the first time anyone has named the rule outright. That night the second voice sings the missing bars perfectly. Beat: dread replacing curiosity.

chapters.title: What Happened in 1974
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Oscar and innkeeper Dan Hobb. Dan, drunk, describes the summer of 1974 when the crops came back from nothing and every child in the village stopped growing older for a year. He won't say what it cost. Beat: the reader learns there was a bargain; Oscar learns she wasn't random.

chapters.title: Elodie
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Parish records reveal a girl, Elodie Amberdale, drowned in the mill pond in October 1974 — same surname, same age Oscar was when she lost her own sister. The second voice says her name into the recorder that night, clearly, twice. Beat: personal stakes ignite.

chapters.title: The Papers
chapters.summary: Dan's POV. A representative of Meridian Development arrives with buyout documents; only Mrs. Tallow's signature remains. Dan explains to Oscar that once the papers are signed, the village will be demolished, paved, and — somehow he knows this — forgotten. Beat: a ticking clock enters the story.

chapters.title: Songs She Never Learned
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar catches herself humming melodies she has never heard, waking with mud on her feet, knowing the layout of a house she's never entered. Her dreams are becoming Elodie's memories. Beat: identity erosion; love against duty begins as Oscar starts to feel protective of the dead girl.

chapters.title: The Chapel Floor
chapters.summary: Dan's POV. Dan confesses that in 1974 his father led the group that drowned Elodie, and that they buried her hymnbook beneath the chapel floorboards to bind the bargain — 'a song given back keeps the giver silent.' He shows Oscar the loose board. Beat: guilt inherited, not chosen.

chapters.title: Meridian's Man
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The developer's representative, Pryce, is revealed to know far too much about Hollowmere's history — his firm has bought three other 'bargain villages' before, and each purchase required the memory to die cleanly. He offers Oscar money to leave early. Beat: power and corruption made corporate and banal.

chapters.title: The Mill Pond
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At night the pond calls her; she walks to its edge and sees Elodie standing on the water, mouth moving in hymn-shape. The voice, through the recorder left on the bank, asks: 'Will you give it back?' Oscar says yes before she understands what she's agreeing to. Beat: commitment; point of no return approached.

chapters.title: Mrs. Tallow Signs
chapters.summary: Dan's POV. Mrs. Tallow, the last holdout, signs the papers after Pryce shows her photographs of her long-dead daughter — leverage no honest man would have. The demolition date is set: eleven days. Beat: despair; the clock accelerates and the village's protectors begin turning on each other.

chapters.title: Villagers
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The remaining residents, sensing the bargain fraying, turn hostile — they slash her tires, steal her recorder, and warn her that outsiders who meddle stay. But old Mr. Fen secretly returns the recorder with a note: 'She was my student. She loved that hymn.' Beat: fear and complicity; one flicker of courage.

chapters.title: The Hymn Complete
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Listening to fifty years of accumulated tapes, Oscar reconstructs the full hymn from fragments — and realizes it isn't a prayer of binding but a lullaby of release, sung wrong in 1974 by frightened people who turned comfort into a cage. Beat: thematic revelation; the ritual was corrupted love.

chapters.title: Pryce's Precedents
chapters.summary: Dan's POV. Dan breaks into Pryce's car and finds files on the three previous villages: in each, a 'custodian' was left behind when the memory died — a person who became the thing that remembers, alone forever. One file lists a custodian still living. Beat: Oscar understands what 'giving it back' truly costs.

chapters.title: The Custodian of Wrenlow
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar tracks down the Wrenlow custodian, a woman in her nineties who has not been seen by another soul in thirty years and cannot forget a single detail of her erased town. She begs Oscar: 'Don't take her place unless you mean it. Memory without love is just punishment.' Beat: the cost made flesh; duty vs. love crystallized.

chapters.title: What Oscar Won't Give Up
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar tries to find a loophole — burn the book, move the grave, destroy the papers — and each attempt fails violently, the village itself resisting. Elodie appears in daylight now, sitting on Oscar's bed, singing softly. They talk, properly, for the first time. Beat: tenderness deepens the horror; Oscar falls in love with the ghost's personhood.

chapters.title: Demolition Eve
chapters.summary: Dan's POV. Machines arrive at the village edge. Dan, breaking with fifty years of his family's silence, stands in front of the chapel and refuses to move; half the remaining residents join him. Pryce watches from his car, making a phone call. Beat: open defiance; the community chooses memory over survival.

chapters.title: The Taking Back
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Under the chapel floor, Oscar lifts the board and takes the hymnbook — waterlogged, warm, beating faintly like a heart. The village goes silent in a way silence shouldn't work; birds stop mid-flight. Elodie's voice, everywhere now, says: 'Bring it to the pond.' Beat: climax begins; the world holds its breath.

chapters.title: Hymn at the Water
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, with Elodie present. At the mill pond, Oscar sings the hymn correctly — as a lullaby of release — and offers the book back. Elodie can cross only if someone agrees to remember in her stead. Oscar, choosing love over self-preservation, accepts. Elodie touches her face, says thank you, and comes apart like light on water. Beat: climax and sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Last Resident Signs
chapters.summary: Dan's POV. Mrs. Tallow tears up her signature; Pryce's machinery withdraws overnight, contracts voided by a clause no one can find in any copy. The village exhales. Dan buries the returned hymnbook properly, above ground, under a stone with Elodie's name spelled right. Beat: resolution; the bargain dissolved by grief done honestly.

chapters.title: What Remembers
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar stays in Hollowmere as its custodian — not punished but purposeful, keeper of every song, every name, every story the outside world will never want. She records herself singing each hymn twice, deliberately, joyfully. Elodie visits sometimes, at the pond's edge, listening. Beat: bittersweet transformation; love fulfilled in duty freely chosen.

chapters.title: Coda: The Recording You Are Hearing
chapters.summary: Epilogue, framed as a transcript of Oscar's final tape, addressed to whoever finds it decades hence. She explains the village, the girl, the choice, and asks only one thing of the listener: sing it back. The tape ends with two voices, in harmony, finishing the hymn together. Beat: haunting closure; memory passed hand to hand.
